1282.title: The disease of arrogance
1282.hook: no one with an atom's weight of arrogance enters the garden, and arrogance is rejecting truth and looking down on people (Muslim)
1282.howItsDone: Muslim teachers count kibr, arrogance, among the diseases of the heart, using the hadith in Sahih Muslim that defines it as rejecting the truth and looking down on people; accepting correction is a common way of working against it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the heart as a lump of flesh, and your line: if the heart is sound. Today, that heart's diseases begin, one at a time.

A gathering in Medina. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says that no one with an atom's weight of arrogance in his heart will enter the garden. A man in the room has a worry, and says it out loud. A man likes his clothes to be good, he says, and his sandals to be good. Is that it? Is a nice pair of sandals what keeps a person out? It's an honest question, and the answer, recorded in Sahih Muslim, is a definition that fits on a sticky note. Today's word: kibr, arrogance.

The answer comes in two halves. First: Allah is beautiful and loves beauty. So the sandals are fine; caring how you look, owning something well made, isn't what the hadith means. Second, the definition: kibr is rejecting the truth and looking down on people. Two motions of the heart. Rejecting the truth is hearing something right and pushing it away, because of who said it, or because agreeing would cost face. Looking down on people is treating someone as smaller than you. Notice what isn't on the list: money, looks, talent. The Qur'an gives a picture of it in Iblis, the one who would not bow, back on day twenty-four. His reason is a comparison: I am better than him, you made me from fire and him from clay. Before the refusal, a ranking. Then Luqman's advice to his son, a father talking to a child: don't turn your cheek away from people in scorn, don't strut on the earth, and, in Pickthall's words, "Lo! Allah loveth not each braggart boaster." The cheek and the walk: arrogance shows in the body. And the cure for the first half is small. Someone corrects you, and they're right. You say: you're right. Before the defense, before the but. A sound heart has room in it for being wrong.
screen: `GOOD SANDALS ARE NOT THE PROBLEM.` · `REJECTING TRUTH, LOOKING DOWN.` · `IBLIS: I AM BETTER THAN HIM.` · then, large: `THE CHEEK AND THE WALK.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a time someone told you that you were wrong, and they had a point: a coworker, a child, a sibling, a stranger in traffic. Notice where the pushing away happened, the jaw, the tone, the quick reply, and quietly give the answer you didn't give then: they were right about that. If you pray, you can ask to be kept from kibr; if you don't, simply rest in the plain fact of it.
Kibr. Arrogance; in the hadith, rejecting the truth and looking down on people. Not good sandals. Today's word.
Your line: reject pride, not truth. Good sandals were never the problem. Tomorrow, a quieter disease: envy.

1283.title: The disease of envy
1283.hook: envy eats good deeds as fire eats wood (Abu Dawud)
1283.howItsDone: Muslims seek refuge from envy in Surah al-Falaq, and teachers distinguish hasad, wishing a blessing gone, from ghibtah, wishing for the same good; praying for the person one envies is a remedy often taught.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kibr, arrogance: rejecting the truth and looking down on people. Your line: reject pride, not truth.

Dry wood in a fire doesn't get a little smaller. It goes. Log, flame, ash. A hadith in Sunan Abu Dawud borrows that picture: the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is reported to have warned against envy, because it eats up good deeds the way fire eats wood. Not dents them. Eats them. Strange, because envy doesn't do anything to anyone. It's a feeling about someone else's life, scrolling past. And yet here it burns the envier's own woodpile. Today's word: hasad, envy.
screen: `DRY WOOD IN A FIRE.` → `IT EATS GOOD DEEDS.` → `HASAD.`

segments.voice: Start where the Qur'an starts. Al-Falaq, a short surah near the end, asks refuge from several things, and one is this, in Pickthall's words: "And from the evil of the envier when he envieth." Now the careful part. Scholars draw a line between two wishes. Hasad is wishing someone's blessing were taken away from them. Wanting the same good too, without wanting it gone from them, they call ghibtah. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari even uses the word envy for that second kind: no envy, it says, except toward a person given wealth who spends it rightly, and a person given wisdom who judges by it and teaches it. So wanting to be like someone good isn't the disease. Wanting them brought down is. You saw that wish early on, in Joseph's brothers, back on day fifty-six. Then the Qur'an goes one level earlier, to the wanting itself: "And covet not the thing in which Allah hath made some of you excel others." And the cure. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says that when a Muslim prays for a brother who isn't there, an angel answers: and for you the same. The prayer for the person you envy lands on you too. Fire eats wood. A prayer for them adds to the pile.
screen: `REFUGE FROM THE ENVIER.` · `WANTING IT GONE, OR WANTING IT TOO.` · `COVET NOT.` · then, large: `AND FOR YOU THE SAME.`

segments.voice: Let one name come up: the friend with the easy job, the cousin with the house, the stranger online whose life looks finished and framed. Notice the tightness the name brings, and don't argue with it. If you pray, ask in your own words that their good thing stay with them and grow; if you don't, simply hold the wish that it go well for them, keeping the name and dropping the comparison.
Hasad. Envy; wishing someone's blessing were taken from them. Wanting the same good without wanting it gone is called ghibtah. Today's word.
Your line: pray for them. And for you the same. Next, the disease that hides inside good deeds.

1284.title: Showing off
1284.howItsDone: Muslim teachers warn against riya', doing good to be seen, starting from the hadith that actions are by intentions; some keep part of their charity and extra prayer private, while public giving is also praised in the Qur'an.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hasad, envy: wishing someone's blessing gone. Your line: pray for them.

Who was watching the last time you did something good? A door held, a donation, a long prayer, a kind comment under someone's post. Sometimes nobody saw. Sometimes the whole room did. The deed looks the same either way. A short surah of the Qur'an, al-Ma'un, turns on exactly this. It speaks of worshippers who pray, and still says woe to them, because of why they pray. Today, the disease that can live inside a good deed: showing off, what Arabic calls riya'.

First, a callback to ikhlas, four days ago: actions are by intentions, the hadith that opens Sahih al-Bukhari. Riya' is the same good deed, aimed at the wrong eyes. Second, the surah. Pickthall's words: "Ah, woe unto worshippers Who are heedless of their prayer; Who would be seen (at worship)". Then the twist: they would be seen, and yet they refuse small kindnesses. The prayer done for an audience sits right next to a hand that won't pass the salt. Showing off and stinginess keep company. Third, a picture from al-Baqarah. Charity given to be seen by people is like a smooth rock with a little soil on it. Heavy rain comes, and the rock is left bare. Nothing could take root. Fourth, the cure, which is not hiding everything. The Qur'an praises those who give by night and by day, in secret and openly; public good can teach and invite. But a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari describes a person Allah shades on a day with no other shade: someone who gives charity so quietly that the left hand doesn't know what the right hand gave. So the practice isn't never be seen. It's keeping a few good deeds where only Allah sees them, so the heart remembers who they were for.
screen: `BY INTENTIONS.` · `WHO WOULD BE SEEN.` · `SOIL ON A SMOOTH ROCK.` · then, large: `THE LEFT HAND DOESN'T KNOW.`

segments.voice: Choose one good thing you could do that nobody will find out about: paying for something anonymously, fixing what someone else broke and saying nothing, praying a little longer when no one is near. See it done, notice the small itch to mention it later, and let the itch be. If you pray, you can ask that it be accepted; if you don't, let the deed be enough without a witness.
Showing off. Riya': doing good in order to be seen; in the Qur'an, soil on a smooth rock that the rain washes away. Today's word.
Your line: not for eyes. The left hand doesn't need to know. Tomorrow, a disease that burns hot and fast: anger.

1285.title: The fire of anger
1285.hook: don't be angry, said three times (Bukhari)
1285.howItsDone: Muslims are taught to answer anger by sitting or lying down, making wudu, and seeking refuge in Allah from Satan, following hadith reports; restraining anger and forgiving are praised in the Qur'an.

segments.voice: Yesterday, showing off: doing good in order to be seen. Your line: not for eyes.

A man comes to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, with a simple request. Advise me. Not a question about law, or the end of the world. Just something to carry. The answer is short. Don't be angry. The man asks again, maybe hoping for something bigger. Don't be angry. He asks again. The same answer, every time. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps the whole exchange, repetitions and all. Today's word: ghadab, anger.

First, what the advice can't mean. Anger arrives on its own; nobody chooses the first flash. So the hadith is about what happens next. Another hadith in al-Bukhari makes that plain: the strong one isn't the one who throws people in wrestling, but the one who controls himself when he's angry. Strength, moved from the arms to the moment after the flash. Second, the Qur'an praises those who do exactly that, in Pickthall's words: "those who control their wrath and are forgiving toward mankind." Control first, then forgiveness. Anger isn't denied; it's held. Third, the body. Reports in Sunan Abu Dawud give practical steps. If you're angry while standing, sit down; if it hasn't left, lie down. Another says anger comes from Satan, Satan was made from fire, and fire is put out with water, so when angry, make wudu, the washing before prayer. And in al-Bukhari, when two men were quarreling and one's face had gone red, the Prophet said he knew words that would take it away: seeking refuge in Allah from Satan. Lower the body. Cool the skin. Say the words. Last, why it's called a fire. Fire spreads, and it's hard to call back; what's said in anger tends to outlast the anger. The short advice gets between the spark and whatever it would catch.
screen: `THE STRONG ONE.` · `THOSE WHO CONTROL THEIR WRATH.` · `SIT, LIE DOWN, MAKE WUDU.` · then, large: `BETWEEN THE SPARK AND WHAT IT CATCHES.`

segments.voice: Let a small annoyance come to mind, a slow driver, a message left on read, and notice where the heat starts: chest, face, hands. Feel the chair under you holding your weight; you're already doing the first step, sitting, and if water is near later, you can cool your hands and face. If you pray, you can seek refuge in Allah from Satan, as in the hadith; if not, just let the heat cool.
Ghadab. Anger; the fire the hadith answers with sitting, water and refuge in Allah. Today's word.
Your line: don't be angry. The flash comes on its own; what comes next is yours. That's today, done.

1286.title: The valley of greed
1286.hook: if a person had a valley of gold he'd want two (Bukhari)
1286.howItsDone: Muslim teachers use the hadith of the valley of gold and the teaching that true richness is richness of the soul to warn against greed; contentment, called qana'ah, and gratitude are practiced as its cure.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ghadab, anger, and your line: don't be angry. The strong one holds it after the flash.

A valley full of gold. Not a bag of it, not a vault. A whole valley, ridge to ridge, glittering in the sun. Surely that's the end of wanting. Surely a person standing on that ridge says: done. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari answers in one plain sentence. If the son of Adam had a valley of gold, he would want a second one. The valley doesn't fill the want. It teaches the want to count. Today: the valley of greed.
screen: `A WHOLE VALLEY OF GOLD.` → `SURELY THAT'S ENOUGH.` → `HE'D WANT A SECOND.`

segments.voice: First, the shape of greed in this hadith. It isn't hunger for one thing; it's a want that grows with the having. Thirst closes when it's met: you drink, it's over. Greed, as the hadith draws it, opens wider when you feed it. Second, the line that follows: nothing fills the mouth of the son of Adam except dust. The dust of the grave. Only the end of a life ends that wanting. But the hadith doesn't stop on dust: and Allah turns to whoever turns to him. The sentence ends on a door, not a grave. Third, the Qur'an says it in two short lines, in Pickthall's words: "Rivalry in worldly increase distracteth you Until ye come to the graves." Rivalry, increase, graves: the same race, stopping only at the end. And fourth, the cure, which the hadith doesn't put in poverty. The valley isn't the disease; the wanting is. Another hadith in al-Bukhari moves the riches somewhere else: richness isn't having many things. Richness is richness of the soul. So enough isn't a number in a bank account. It's a place in the heart where the wanting can sit down.
screen: `A WANT THAT GROWS WITH HAVING.` · `ONLY DUST FILLS IT.` · `RIVALRY IN WORLDLY INCREASE.` · then, large: `RICHNESS OF THE SOUL.`

segments.voice: Start with the breath: it came, and it was enough for this moment; then the seat under you, the last thing you ate, the roof overhead, one person who'd pick up if you called. Name each one quietly, and after each, the word: enough. When the mind reaches for the next thing on the list, notice the reach and come back; if you pray, you can thank Allah for one of them by name.
The valley of greed. The hadith's picture of a want that grows with having: a valley of gold, and a wish for a second. Today's word.
Your line: enough is enough. Richness is richness of the soul. See you tomorrow, for the harm of backbiting.

1287.title: The harm of backbiting
1287.hook: mentioning your brother with what he'd dislike (Muslim)
1287.howItsDone: Muslims are taught to avoid ghibah, speaking of an absent person in a way they would dislike even if it is true, following Sahih Muslim and Qur'an 49:12; scholars allow naming faults for specific needs such as seeking help against injustice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the valley of greed, and your line: enough is enough. A want that grows with the having.

Do you know what backbiting is? The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, put that question to his companions, and Sahih Muslim records it. They answered the way people answer a teacher they trust: Allah and his Messenger know best. So he told them. Backbiting is mentioning your brother with something he would dislike. Then someone asked the question group chats ask sooner or later. But what if it's true? What if I'm only saying what he really did? Today: the harm of backbiting, and the answer.
screen: `DO YOU KNOW WHAT IT IS?` → `WHAT HE WOULD DISLIKE.` → `BUT WHAT IF IT'S TRUE?`

segments.voice: The answer is the surprise. If what you say about him is true, that is backbiting. If it isn't true, that's something else, buhtan, slander. So truth isn't a defense here; truth is the definition. The test is whether he'd dislike hearing it said behind his back. Second, the Qur'an's picture, a hard one, first met on day five hundred eighty-seven. In Pickthall's words: "neither backbite one another. Would one of you love to eat the flesh of his dead brother? Ye abhor that". The image is meant to turn the stomach. Some readers notice a detail: the dead can't answer back, and neither can someone who isn't in the room. Third, the honest exceptions. Scholars such as an-Nawawi listed cases where naming someone's fault is allowed: asking for help against a wrong done to you, seeking a ruling, warning someone about a real danger. In a hadith in al-Bukhari, a woman named Hind told the Prophet that her husband didn't give her enough to live on, and he answered her question. Naming a fault to fix a harm is different from naming it for the pleasure of the telling. And last, why it's easy: backbiting bonds people. Two friends, a third one absent, and suddenly there's a topic. The way out is another topic.
screen: `WHAT HE WOULD DISLIKE.` · `IF IT'S TRUE, IT'S STILL BACKBITING.` · `THE FLESH OF A DEAD BROTHER.` · then, large: `TO FIX A HARM, NOT FOR THE TELLING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people you're most likely to talk about, a boss, an in-law, a friend who's been difficult, and one at a time, picture them walking in while you're speaking about them. Whatever you'd stop saying when they walked in, that's the line. Prepare one way out, a change of subject, a kind word about them, or simply silence, and if you pray, you can ask for help guarding the tongue.
The harm of backbiting. Ghibah: mentioning someone with what they'd dislike, even when it's true. When it's false, it's slander. Today's word.
Your line: not behind their backs. If they'd mind hearing it, it can wait. Tomorrow, two roads, and one of them is lying.

1288.title: The road of lying
1288.hook: truthfulness leads to goodness, lying to wickedness (Bukhari)
1288.howItsDone: Muslims are taught truthfulness, sidq, as a habit that leads to goodness, following the hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari; teachers warn against small lies too, including the coaxing lies told to children.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the harm of backbiting, and your line: not behind their backs. True and unwelcome still counts.

A road doesn't have to be steep to take you somewhere. One step, then the next, and an hour later you're in another town without ever deciding to move there. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari describes two roads like that. On one, a person keeps telling the truth. On the other, a person keeps lying. Neither looks dramatic from the first step. Both arrive somewhere. Today, the next disease on the path: the road of lying.
screen: `ONE STEP, THEN THE NEXT.` → `TWO ROADS.` → `BOTH ARRIVE SOMEWHERE.`

segments.voice: Here is the hadith, in plain English. Truthfulness leads to goodness, and goodness leads to the garden. A person keeps telling the truth until he is written with Allah as truthful. And lying leads to wickedness, and wickedness leads to the fire. A person keeps lying until he is written with Allah as a liar. Notice the word keeps. It's about which road the feet are used to. Second, how small the steps can be. In a report in Sunan Abu Dawud, a mother calls her little boy over: come here, I'll give you something. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is in the house and asks what she meant to give him. Some dates, she says. And he tells her that if she'd given him nothing, it would have been written against her as a lie. A coaxing line to a child. That small. Third, company. In Pickthall's words: "O ye who believe! Be careful of your duty to Allah, and be with the truthful." Truth is easier to walk with others. And last, a reading some teachers offer: under several of these diseases sits a small lie the heart tells. I'm better. They don't deserve it. Watch me. I'm owed. Not enough. Did you hear what she did. The road of truth starts with telling yourself the truth first.
screen: `TWO ROADS, TWO ENDINGS.` · `KEEPS TELLING THE TRUTH.` · `A HANDFUL OF DATES.` · then, large: `BE WITH THE TRUTHFUL.`

segments.voice: Walk through the day ahead and find where the small ones usually live: I'm five minutes away, I love it, I didn't see your message. Choose a true version now, kind and short: I'm running late, it's not for me but thank you, I saw it and needed time. If you pray, you can ask to be written among the truthful; if not, just hold the true sentence ready.
The road of lying. The hadith's picture of habit: lie after lie leads to wickedness, and truth after truth leads to goodness and the garden. Today's word.
Your line: truth leads to good. The word that matters is keeps. Back tomorrow, same hill.
